# Models, tuning and the one-shot test {#sec-modeling} ## Splitting by time A random 80/20 split leaks the future: the model would train on November and "predict" September, already knowing how the season turned out. So every split is **by time**: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Train, validation and test by season, and the walk-forward cross-validation folds inside the training window.](modeling_files/figure-pdf/fig-split-output-1.pdf){#fig-split} ::: ::: | Set | Seasons | Used for | |---|---|---| | Train | 2016–2023 (2015 only feeds features) | Fitting; cross-validation and Optuna run only here | | Validation | 2024 | Choosing the final model and ensemble | | Test | 2025 | Touched **once**, at the end: the honest number | | Production | 2026 | Weekly predictions | : Data splits. {#tbl-splits} Cross-validation is **walk-forward**: train on every season before, validate on the next, for 2019 through 2023. Each fold weighs the same. ## The model zoo and tuning Every model predicts points per team. Tree models learn the **residual of the ratings** ($\text{points} - \text{exp\_points}$), the shape that won the ablations; linear models predict points directly. Each was tuned with Optuna's TPE sampler [@akiba_optuna], minimizing walk-forward MAE, starting from hand-picked defaults. ::: {.callout-note} ## How tuning and cross-validation fit together For **each of the six models**, Optuna proposes a set of hyperparameters (one *trial*). That trial is scored with **walk-forward cross-validation**: the model is trained on the seasons before 2019 and validated on 2019, retrained through 2019 and validated on 2020, and so on through 2023. The trial's score is the average of those five errors. Optuna uses the scores to propose better trials (15 to 60 per model). The best trial per model is saved to `models/team_points_params.json`. Only after that are the six tuned models combined and compared on 2024, and only the final choice is tested on 2025. The half and quarter models reuse LightGBM's tuned parameters rather than being tuned separately. ::: ::: {#tbl-tuning .cell tbl-cap='Optuna results (mean per-season CV MAE, 2019–2023). Read live from models/team_points_params.json.' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Every model lands within ~0.05 points of the others, and their errors are almost perfectly correlated (≥ 0.98). They see the same information and make the same mistakes, so an ensemble can only help a little. Ridge's best $\alpha$ (978) sits at the edge of its search range (up to 1000), which is noted but doesn't change the conclusion. ## Ensembles, validation and the final pick Out-of-fold predictions from the five CV folds fed three ensembles: a simple average, the average of the top 3, and **stacking** with non-negative least squares. The stacking weights (ridge 0.45, XGBoost 0.33, Poisson 0.10, LightGBM 0.06, random forest 0.04, CatBoost 0) were fit on the same out-of-fold rows, so their CV number is slightly optimistic. That's why the final choice is made on 2024. | Model | OOF 2019–23 (pooled) | Validation 2024 | Test 2025 | |---|---|---|---| | **Random forest (final: best on 2024)** | 9.275 | **9.081** | **8.940** | | Stacking (NNLS) | 9.200 | 9.097 | | | Average of all six | 9.212 | 9.085 | | | XGBoost (best in CV) | 9.236 | 9.133 | | | Market: opening line | | 8.869 | 8.696 | | Market: closing line | | 8.861 | 8.594 | : Model selection and the one-shot test (copied from the experiment log). {#tbl-test} The final recipe, random\_forest, won 2024 by a margin that's within noise. Any of the top candidates would have been defensible. The **2025 test was run once**, with everything frozen beforehand. **Verdict on accuracy:** the market is better by ~0.25 points per team, both at the open and at the close. ## The market layer, and why it was dropped Opening lines only exist from 2021, too few seasons to train a full model against the market. So the points model stays market-blind, and a tiny logistic regression (inputs: the edge vs the opener, the edge × early season, and the size of the line) was fit on 2021–2023 to learn *when* to trust the model's disagreement with the opener. - **Spreads:** 47–49% in the 2025 test. It doesn't work. - **Totals:** 55.7% in 2025 at $p \ge 0.5$. But its coefficient on the model's edge came out **negative**, so it wasn't using the model at all; it mostly bet unders on high totals. That was first read as a pure base-rate artifact of an under-heavy 2025. The nonlinearity analysis later showed it's partly a stable effect (@sec-nonlinearity), which is now a separate, explicit rule. The layer was dropped from the weekly card. Its useful part lives on as rule B. ::: {.callout-note} ## What changed after the test The 2025 test above used the features up to `priors`. Later, preseason features were adopted under the anti-overfitting rule (decided on 2021–2023, confirmed on 2024–2025; @sec-improvements), and the production model uses them. The report card (@sec-reportcard) reflects the current model. :::
